item.title: Hadj Moussa sinks Como as Feyenoord claim first CL group win
item.description:
Hadj Moussa sinks Como as Feyenoord claim first CL group win

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Feyenoord claimed the first win for the Eredivisie teams in the Champions League as they got the better of Italian upstarts Como 1907 in a five-goal thriller.

After a cagey opening, Como took the lead when Assane Diao won a physical challenge on the left with Javi Lopez and drilled the ball past Tjark Ernst from a tight angle.

Feyenoord were level within two minutes as Gjivai Zechiël span away from his marker on the edge of the penalty area and lofted a shot into the top corner.

The visitors suffered a setback when Diao limped off a few minutes later, while Feyenoord grew in confidence, with Givairo Read and Lopez drawing fingertip saves from Como goalkeeper Robert Sanchez just before half-time.

Feyenoord went ahead with the first real chance after the interval, as Anis Haji Moussa cut in from the right and found the bottom corner of Sanchez’ net.

Ten minutes from the end the Algerian appeared to have put the result beyond doubt when his long-range shot came back off the post and deflected in off the goalkeeper’s back to make the score 3-1.

Tasos Douvikas’s injury-time strike for Como ensured a tense last few minutes, but Feyenoord were not to be denied.

Zechiël said the quick reply after Diao put the visitors ahead was crucial for his teammates’ morale. “That gave the team and the stadium the feeling we were going to win today.”

He was full of praise for Hadj Moussa, who had a decisive role in both second-half goals. “Anis is a top-class player. We’re really pleased that he’s still available for us this season.”

The result lifts Feyenoord to 23rd place in the 36-team table, while their next match is a trip to Real Betis next Wednesday, October 21.

item.title: Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law
item.description:
Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

International workers, students and family migrants will no longer be entitled to penalty payments when the immigration service IND misses its deadlines, the asylum ministry has said after a new law was passed by the senate on Tuesday.

The change was presented as an asylum measure, but a ministry spokesperson told Dutch News the law applies to applications for regular residence permits, including highly skilled migrants, students and family members.

The IND is supposed to make a decision on a residence application within 6 months. If it misses that deadline, applicants can go to court to demand a payment for every day it remains late. Once the new law takes effect, judges will only be able to order the IND to reach a decision within a set period.

The government abandoned plans to axe penalty payments for regular residence applicants in 2024, saying it could conflict with EU law. The ministry told us it could not yet say what had changed.

Asylum minister Bart van den Brink told MPs in September the IND had paid out close to €100 million in penalties, noting that some asylum applicants had ended up receiving over €100,000. The IND also insists these penalties do nothing to speed things up.

A spokesperson from the IND told Dutch News the service does not currently know how much in penalty payments is paid for regular permit applicants, but it will calculate the figures in the coming weeks.

D66, which voted against the asylum package in April, backed the new law. In April, D66 senator Boris Dittrich told Dutch News the party opposed the package because it would have made living in the country without valid papers a criminal offence. That measure is not part of the new law.

A D66 spokesperson acknowledged that the IND’s failure to meet deadlines “is not resolved by this amendment”, but told us on Tuesday the penalties “no longer provide an incentive to work more efficiently and have therefore outlived their purpose”.

“In our view, abolishing the penalty payments must go hand in hand with measures aimed at the ultimate goal: faster procedures, so that everyone who comes here receives clarity as quickly as possible,” the spokesperson said.

item.title: Former Groningen mayor loses appeal against indecency conviction
item.description:
Former Groningen mayor loses appeal against indecency conviction

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The former mayor of Groningen, Koen Schuiling, has lost his appeal against a conviction for offending public decency that led to him being forced to take early retirement two years ago.

Judges upheld a €250 fine imposed by a court in Zwolle after he was found guilty of masturbating in his car on the A7 motorway in the city.

He was reported to police by a passing lorry driver, but insisted when questioned that he had stopped to relieve stomach complaints caused by a medical condition.

The court found that the driver had a clear view of Schuiling’s car and had given an detailed and consistent account of what he saw. His testimony was corroborated by an audio recording made in the cab in which he could be heard angrily challenging Schuiling about his behaviour.

Schuiling stepped down from his post in September 2024, a year before his term of office was due to end. At the time he said he lacked energy after an “extraordinarily intense period” that included the coronavirus lockdowns and the rollout of compensation to homeowners in Groningen who were affected by earthquake damage.

But it soon emerged that home affairs minister Judith Uitermark demanded his resignation after she was briefed by the police and public prosecutor about the allegations against Schuiling, arguing it exposed him to blackmail.

Police had received two earlier complaints in the previous six months about the mayor behaving inappropriately at the wheel of his vehicle.

item.title: Van Essen dismisses farmers’ alternative nitrogen emissions plan
item.description:
Van Essen dismisses farmers’ alternative nitrogen emissions plan

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen has dismissed an alternative plan to solve the nitrogen pollution crisis presented by farmers’ organisations, arguing it would lead to legal challenges.

Four organisations under the banner of the Landbouw Alliantie (“Agricultural Alliance”) called for the cabinet to adopt its more limited programme of reforms as a basis for negotiations.

The farmers want the Netherlands to implement a German-style system with exclusion zones of 250m around protected nature areas rather than 500m or 1,000m, so that fewer farmers would have to reduce their cattle herds.

But Van Essen said the plans were not a realistic route out of the crisis. “The Netherlands will not end the impasse by weakening measures in places where nature needs it most and at the same time relaxing the rules for permits.”

He said the package of measures announced by the government in June remained “the basis” for discussions with the agriculture sector. The left-wing opposition party Pro, whose support is key to passing the legislation, has also warned that the plan “must not be weakened”.

“Paper problem”

Sieta van Keimpema, of the Dutch Dairy Board (DDB), one of four organisations that make up the Landbouw Alliantie, said the government should rewrite the rules to allow more generous limits, as in Germany. “It is a paper problem, so we should be able to come up with a paper solution,” she said.

But farmers also face the prospect of legal challenges from environmental groups such as Mobilisation for the Environment, which has raised cases in 10 provinces against 130 farms that have breached nitrogen deposition limits.

Van Essen’s plans aim to reduce nitrogen compound emissions from farming by up to 46% and by 50% for other high-polluting sectors such as heavy industry and transport.

The most vulnerable conservation zones will be protected by 1km exclusion zones, where farmers will have to abide by strict pollution limits, while another 85 nature areas will be surrounded by 500m zones.

The reforms were triggered by a Council of State ruling in 2019 that struck down the system for issuing nature permits for large construction projects such as roads, suburbs and extensions to farms.

Until then permits were issued if applicants could show that the nitrogen generated during construction would be offset by efficiencies made by the finished project. But the Council of State said nitrogen limits had to be adhered to during building work as well.

item.title: No more Dolphins in NL: government moves to ban breeding
item.description:
No more Dolphins in NL: government moves to ban breeding

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dolphin breeding is to be banned in the Netherlands within two years, and imports of the animals will be restricted.

Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens told parliament in a letter on Wednesday that keeping dolphins in captivity prevents them from expressing their natural behaviour and can cause health problems.

“Dolphins are intelligent animals that need to be constantly challenged and have a natural need to be able to dive deep and swim long distances,” said Erkens. “That cannot be provided in captivity. Life in chlorinated pools can also cause health problems.”

An immediate ban on dolphin captivity is not wanted because it would mean killing 22 bottlenose dolphins at the country’s Dolfinarium in Harderwijk, Gelderland.

But eventually, by preventing breeding and limiting importation, captivity for entertainment or education will be phased out entirely. The Dolfinarium criticised the cabinet, saying breeding is an essential aspect of welfare and will damage the dolphins’ health.

item.title: Newcomers face tougher Dutch standards, but some see opportunity
item.description:
Partner content

Newcomers face tougher Dutch standards, but some see opportunity

October 14, 2026

The Netherlands has raised the level of Dutch it expects from newcomers. For those who reach B1, the payoff goes beyond the paperwork. We spoke with experts at language school Language Corner about how the change in requirements is both a challenge and an opportunity for the international community.

Foreigners in the Netherlands are increasingly expected to speak Dutch at an intermediate level, as the government moves the standard from the basic A2 level to the more advanced B1.

For those who have to meet it, that means more time and money spent in the classroom. But learners and teachers say the higher level also brings people closer to working and living in the Netherlands.

For many, B1 is already the norm. Since January 1, 2022, people covered by the Civic Integration Act 2021 – mainly refugees and family members joining a partner here – have had to aim for B1 as part of their integration (inburgering) programme.

They can drop down to A2 only after making what the rules call “significant effort”, including 600 hours of lessons, according to municipal social services association Divosa.

Citizenship next
Citizenship is the next step; for now, people who want to naturalise can still do so with an A2 integration diploma. EU, EEA and Swiss nationals are largely exempt.

But the coalition of D66, the VVD and CDA has written a B1 requirement into its January coalition agreement, as part of a new route to citizenship for people on temporary residence permits.

The pledge is not new. The Rutte III, Rutte IV and Schoof cabinets all promised to raise the language bar for naturalisation to B1, and none put it into effect.

A2 versus B1
Both levels come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, the scale used across Europe to measure language skills.

At A2, a “basic user” can handle simple, routine exchanges on familiar topics such as shopping, family and directions. At B1, an “independent user” can follow the main points of clear, standard speech about work, school and leisure, and deal with most everyday situations.

B1 speakers can also write simple connected texts, describe experiences and give reasons for their opinions. In practice, that means considerably more study than A2.

The opportunities 
The rules are not the only reason to aim higher. Carlos Blasco, a design engineer from Valencia who has taken two courses at Amsterdam language school Language Corner, said he has noticed a shift in the job market.

“When I moved here three years ago, Dutch wasn’t really a requirement,” he said. “Nowadays, I see it in almost every job offer, so I think it makes professional sense to improve my Dutch.”

Blasco is now on a B1 course. He said he is learning to integrate into local life as much as for work.

Exam preparation
Language Corner, which teaches Dutch at two locations in Amsterdam and online, said many of its students switch to private lessons once they reach A2, to prepare for the B1 exams.

“Private lessons can really focus on an individual’s situation,” said Eric van Heesen of Language Corner. “In addition to prepping for the B1 exams, private lessons can help students improve where they need to, whether it’s speaking, listening or grammar.”

Teacher Daniel Vis said some students need B1 for a specific goal. “Some want to learn something specific, like studying for a master’s degree, in which case you need to be at the B1 level,” he said. “For such specifics, private lessons are better, because we do intensive course work with them.”

Edward Blake, an American experience designer, took group classes before moving to one-to-one lessons. “We had conversations, gave presentations, played games, wrote short papers and even watched a bit of broadcaster NPO,” he said.

Outside the classroom
The school also runs social gatherings outside lessons. Vis said he took his students to watch the recent eclipse, and they spoke Dutch together.

Blake, who said he chose classroom lessons over online or AI-based learning, is measuring his progress in daily life. “I’m faultless in an ice cream shop, but that skill has become less useful as the weather turns,” he said. “I try reading the Dutch newspapers but to mixed success (for now). I’m getting there.”

For Blasco, the turning point came at the Lowlands festival this summer, where there were few internationals. “I got to practise a lot of Dutch, and people – contrary to before – didn’t switch to English,” he said.

He said he can now follow conversations on the street and the news. “I might still miss some nuances, but that’ll come with time.”

If you’re just starting your language journey or need to pass your B1 levels, check out the Dutch course offerings at Language Corner.

item.title: Jetten attacks Trump’s diesel deal as “unwise” and pointless
item.description:
Jetten attacks Trump’s diesel deal as “unwise” and pointless

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has urged US president Donald Trump to ditch the “diesel deal” with Russia, arguing it will harm not just Ukraine but its allies in Europe and America.

During a debate in parliament on Tuesday, Jetten called the deal “unwise” and said it was based on flawed reasoning, because it will not drive down pump prices in the US in time for next month’s midterm Congressional elections.

“The idea that buying more diesel from Russia will calm the international markets and lower prices for American consumers doesn’t work in practice,” he said. “And certainly not for the midterms, because even if those ships can leave Russia, they won’t reach the American mainland in time.”

Trump announced the deal last week on his own social media platform, Truth Social, boasting it will mean “lower prices for Americans, especially our great farmers, ranchers and truckers”.

He also suspended sanctions against Russia until April 7 and called on Ukraine to stop its missile strikes on Russian oil refineries.

“Investment in war”

The deal was attacked by Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who called it an “investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”.

But experts have said the total amount he agreed to buy from Russia is too small to have a significant impact on prices.

Jetten said: “The ‘diesel deal’ between the United States and Russia is regrettable and very unwise, because every dollar that flows into Russia’s war chest is bad news for Ukraine and all its allies, including the Europeans and the Americans themselves.

“We need to wait and see how this deal is implemented in practice, but the core is that we will continue to support Ukraine and make clear to the Americans that this deal needs to be taken off the table.”

item.title: Auditors: €9.5bn needed to put roads and railways on war footing
item.description:
Auditors: €9.5bn needed to put roads and railways on war footing

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands needs to invest nearly €10 billion to make its road and rail infrastructure fit for war, auditors have warned in a critical report.

The Court of Audit said investment was needed to upgrade motorways and rail lines to ensure military vehicles and supplies can be transported across the country.

“Shortfalls in the maintenance budget mean that on an everyday basis, infrastructure is so outdated that it can no longer be used properly,” the auditors said.

“This leads to limitations on use, such as traffic travelling at lower speeds or with lighter loads, which military transport also has to contend with.”

The Netherlands’ key strategic position on the edge of the North Sea makes it a crucial link in the chain for military supplies to Nato partners. A broken bridge or subsidence on the railway line could have far-reaching consequences, the auditors warned.

Last year junior infrastructure minister Thierry Aartsen called for a review of the railway lines between the Netherlands and the Baltic states, after researchers warned that the network was prone to sabotage.

Railway sabotage

A month ago saboteurs brought the network to a standstill by fastening steel pipes and other objects to rail lines, in a co-ordinated campaign that was blamed on farmers angry with the government’s plans to tackle the nitrogen emissions crisis.

Altogether the audit office says the country needs to spend an extra €9.5bn, including €5 billion to meet Nato standards by widening military corridors, raising clearance heights and strengthening bridges.

They added that the list was incomplete because it does not include spending on waterways or how much was needed to maintain military corridors in their current state.

The figure is far greater than the €1.5bn the cabinet announced in its 2027 budget for repairs to roads and bridges over the next decade. All Nato countries agreed at last year’s summit in The Hague to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP, including 1.5% on critical infrastructure.

item.title: ASML posts record quarter as AI demand outpaces expansion plans
item.description:
ASML posts record quarter as AI demand outpaces expansion plans

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch chip-machine maker ASML had a record third quarter, with sales of €11.7 billion and net profit of €5 billion. That is well up from the €2.1 billion profit last year.

ASML is benefiting from the boom in AI, with customers continuously raising their forecasts for how many machines they will need.

That puts pressure on ASML to make more machines. The company had planned to raise capacity by 30% in 2027, with a possible further 30% in 2028, but now says even that will not fully meet customer demand.

Sales of upgrades for existing machines also rose above expectations, reaching €3.3 billion, helping push the profit margin to 57.5%.

ASML expects fourth-quarter sales of between €14.2 billion and €15.2 billion, and between €44 billion and €45 billion for the full year. Shareholders will receive an interim dividend of €1.88 per share in November.

item.title: VeiligThuis denied plea for extra funding for domestic abuse
item.description:
VeiligThuis denied plea for extra funding for domestic abuse

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Domestic abuse reporting network VeiligThuis had its request for an additional
€70 million rejected by parliament on Tuesday, after the organisation said it was being overwhelmed with reports and could not handle the workload.

Waiting lists have been growing substantially for years, and how a case is handled depends on the region where you live.

MPs voted against immediately granting more money. First, parliament wants the cabinet to look at the “role, position and capacity” of VeiligThuis to see how best to improve it. A motion calling for that investigation was passed a year ago.

MPs agreed the motion needs to be implemented now, but that more money is not the solution until the problems are better understood.

Pro MP Lisa Westerveld said the previous and current cabinets are responsible for the delay. “This is not primarily a matter of money, but of doing what was promised.”

In the past year, serious child abuse incidents have sparked national outrage and drawn attention to the lack of sufficient resources and care.
